title: Developmental Bootstrapping of the BG Optimizer

html:
The preceding sections described the BG’s policy-optimization machinery as though it arrives fully formed: distributional error signals, opponent plasticity, territory-specific loss functions, cholinergic gating, and hierarchical cognitive control all operating in concert. But the BG optimizer does not start from a blank slate, nor does it come online all at once. Its objective function, its teaching-signal infrastructure, and its corticostriatal connectivity are themselves bootstrapped over a protracted developmental timescale that spans from the prenatal specification of dopaminergic pathways through adolescent circuit refinement, with different components of the optimization stack maturing at different rates and in a functionally consequential sequence. This developmental ordering is not incidental; it defines which kinds of policy learning are available at each stage of life and, by implication, which aspects of the organism’s value landscape are laid down first and therefore exert the strongest structural constraint on all subsequent learning.

The initial preference distribution is anchored to homeostatic correction. The BG optimizer’s first operating environment is the neonatal world, in which the only contexts reliably driving strong dopaminergic prediction errors are those that correct acute homeostatic imbalances. In altricial mammals, virtually all early reward structure derives from maternal interaction: milk delivery corrects caloric and fluid depletion, thermal contact resolves cold stress, tactile stimulation regulates autonomic and hormonal milieu. Because these are the events most reliably available in early postnatal life, and because they are intrinsically coupled to interoceptive repletion signals—gastric stretch, rising blood glucose, skin warming, declining cortisol—the first value functions the corticostriatal system learns are necessarily tethered to homeostatic set points. The mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway, comprising VTA projections to the nucleus accumbens and ventral striatum, is functional relatively early in postnatal development: in rodents, dopaminergic fibers reach the striatum and nucleus accumbens by the late embryonic period (approximately E15-E17), and the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic pathways largely complete their basic wiring during the first postnatal week 1, 2. This early functionality means that the mesolimbic system is positioned to generate reward prediction errors in response to homeostatic correction events well before the cortical representations over which those errors are computed have achieved anything approaching adult sophistication. The predictions that VTA GABA neurons and lateral hypothalamic projections encode as the infant’s first conditional expectations are predictions about interoceptive state—about the arrival of milk, warmth, and contact—not about abstract symbolic variables. In this sense, the initial "loss function" of the BG optimizer is defined not by a general-purpose reward-maximization mandate, but by the specific homeostatic error signals that the hypothalamic-VTA architecture is pre-wired to detect. This is not merely a starting condition that is later overwritten; it is a structural constraint that persists throughout life, ensuring that however abstract the BG’s value computations become, they remain tethered to biological viability through the interoceptive grounding of the dopaminergic prediction baseline described at length in the error-signal section 3, 4.

As the infant’s cortical representations mature, the BG gain access to progressively richer state spaces over which to compute value. The developmental trajectory of corticostriatal functional connectivity reflects this expansion with remarkable clarity. In a large resting-state fMRI study spanning ages 3-42, Bhargava and colleagues showed that dorsal striatal connectivity to sensorimotor cortical regions is established early and remains strong through childhood and adolescence, supporting sensory-seeking behaviors and basic habit formation during these developmental periods 5. Connectivity to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex emerged only in adolescence, while connectivity to dorsomedial prefrontal and posterior cortical regions belonging to attentional and default-mode networks was not observed until adulthood 5. This ventral-to-dorsal, sensorimotor-to-associative, and local-to-long-range developmental gradient in corticostriatal connectivity means that the BG’s policy-optimization machinery operates over a progressively expanding cortical state space: early in life, the system can learn policies over sensorimotor and limbic representations (simple stimulus-reward associations, basic approach-avoidance); later, as associative and prefrontal loops come online, it can learn policies over increasingly abstract representations including action-outcome contingencies, task rules, working-memory contents, and strategic variables. Secondary reinforcers–social approval, symbolic reward, abstract goal satisfaction–are not hard-wired but emerge from the same TD learning machinery operating over cortically enriched state representations, constructed through chains of associative and identity prediction errors anchored, ultimately, to the early-established homeostatic baseline. The developmental expansion of the BG optimizer’s computational reach is not driven solely by cortical maturation; it also depends on the maturation of the dopaminergic teaching signal itself, which follows a strikingly pathway-specific timetable. In rodents, the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic dopamine pathways largely complete their basic innervation during the first postnatal week, but the mesocortical dopamine pathway—VTA projections to prefrontal cortex—has a uniquely protracted maturation that continues through adolescence and into early adulthood 1, 6, 2. The density of dopamine fibers in prefrontal regions increases progressively from the late embryonic period through adulthood, a pattern replicated across rodents and primates 2, 6. Remarkably, Reynolds, Bhatt, and colleagues showed using dual viral tracing that a significant subset of mesocortical dopamine axons are still physically growing from the nucleus accumbens to the prefrontal cortex during adolescence–the only known case of long-distance axon growth at this developmental stage (based on the 2017 article)–and that the extent of this growth is regulated by the Netrin-1 guidance cue receptor DCC, which determines target recognition events in axons passing through the striatum 7, 8. This protracted mesocortical maturation has a direct computational implication for the BG optimizer: the cognitive gating functions described in the preceding section–working-memory updating, attentional control, task-set selection, hierarchical rule learning, and meta-learning–depend on dopaminergic modulation of prefrontal circuits, and these circuits are not fully innervated until early adulthood. The BG’s capacity to learn cognitive policies (the PBWM-style gating of prefrontal representations) therefore comes online substantially later than its capacity to learn basic appetitive and sensorimotor policies, potentially explaining why young children can learn simple stimulus-reward associations and motor skills but struggle with tasks requiring flexible cognitive control and abstract rule use.

In parallel with the protracted growth of mesocortical fibers, the dopamine receptor landscape itself undergoes developmental remodeling. In rat dorsal striatum, D1 and D2 receptor densities peak around puberty (approximately postnatal day 28-40) and are subsequently pruned back to adult levels, with reductions of 35-40% from peak values 9, 10. In the nucleus accumbens, by contrast, receptor densities plateau without the same pronounced pruning, suggesting territory-specific developmental trajectories that may differentially shape the learning dynamics of ventral versus dorsal loops during adolescence 9. In prefrontal cortex, the maturation of dopaminergic modulation follows yet another trajectory: before mid-adolescence, D2 receptor stimulation has weak or negligible effects on GABAergic interneuron firing, but after adolescence an excitatory D2 effect on interneurons emerges that creates the inhibitory tone characteristic of the mature prefrontal circuit 2, 1. This adolescent shift in dopaminergic regulation of prefrontal excitation-inhibition balance is thought to be a critical step in the developmental calibration of cognitive control, and its disruption may contribute to psychiatric disorders of adolescent onset 2. A 2026 adolescent rodent study links dopamine-neuron GluN2A to feedback and prediction-error learning (Figure) 15. Adolescent dopamine-neuron plasticity can shape feedback-guided behavior (Figure).

The well-documented adolescent profile–heightened reward sensitivity, increased sensation-seeking, greater risk tolerance, and relatively immature cognitive control–can be read, through the framework developed in this chapter, as a developmental mismatch between components of the BG optimization stack that mature at different rates 11, 12. The ventral striatal/mesolimbic system, which provides the critic-like value scaffolding and motivational drive described in the loss-function and skill-acquisition sections, is functionally mature by early adolescence and shows peak reward reactivity during this period: fMRI studies consistently report that ventral striatal activation to reward anticipation and receipt follows an inverted-U developmental trajectory, peaking in mid-adolescence and declining toward adult levels 11, 13. Meanwhile, the dorsomedial and prefrontal components of the BG optimizer—the associative loops that support goal-directed control, the cognitive gating circuits that implement hierarchical rule use and working-memory management, and the mesocortical dopamine projections that modulate all of these functions—are still maturing, with long-range striatal-prefrontal connectivity not reaching adult patterns until the mid-twenties 5, 14. The result, in the vocabulary of this chapter, is a BG optimizer whose ventral/limbic loss functions and error signals are operating at full gain while its dorsomedial/associative policy-learning and cognitive-gating circuits are still being tuned. The territory-specific loss landscape is, during adolescence, temporarily distorted: the long-horizon, motivationally weighted valuation machinery is fully calibrated, but the intermediate-horizon, contingency-sensitive, and cognitively gated control machinery that normally counterbalances it is still being assembled. This imbalance is not a design flaw; it may be an adaptive feature of a system that must, during a specific developmental window, recalibrate its policy repertoire for the demands of independent adult life—a period in which heightened exploration, novelty-seeking, and sensitivity to social reward serve the organism’s transition from parental dependence to autonomous agency. The composite picture is of a BG optimizer whose developmental trajectory mirrors the hierarchical structure of its adult architecture. The system boots from the bottom up: homeostatic anchoring first (hypothalamic-VTA pre-wiring ensures the first prediction errors are about biological need), mesolimbic reward learning second (ventral striatal value functions are established in infancy), sensorimotor habit learning third (dorsolateral corticostriatal connectivity is strong from early childhood), associative/goal-directed policy learning fourth (dorsomedial-prefrontal connectivity emerges in adolescence), and full cognitive gating last (mesocortical dopamine innervation and prefrontal dopamine receptor maturation are not complete until early adulthood). At each stage, the BG can learn policies only over the state spaces that cortex has made legible and that dopaminergic innervation has made teachable. The developmental curriculum of the BG optimizer is therefore not organized over the type and scope of policy: from rigid homeostatic reflexes, through flexible sensorimotor skills, to abstract cognitive strategies and meta-learning–with each successive layer of policy complexity becoming available only as the required cortical, dopaminergic, and corticostriatal infrastructure comes online. This developmental ordering also implies that the earliest-learned value functions—those anchored to homeostatic correction and primary reward—occupy a privileged position in the BG’s loss landscape: they are laid down first, they shape the dopaminergic baseline against which all subsequent prediction errors are computed, and they are encoded in the most structurally mature corticostriatal circuits. In this sense, the BG optimizer’s "objective function" is not a free parameter specified by experience alone; it is inherited from the survival-critical error signals that first activated the system’s teaching machinery, and this developmental origin is preserved in the structural connectivity between hypothalamic homeostatic controllers and the midbrain dopaminergic nuclei that distribute the credit assignment signal throughout life.
